samples.question: This image shows two flagpoles standing on the same ground line on white paper. Each POLE is one of the two dark grey upright bars, and the CENTRE LINE of a pole is the straight up-and-down line through the middle of that bar. Each pole carries exactly one FLAG: a solid triangle of colour attached to the pole and reaching sideways from it. The two flags are the only coloured marks on the page and each flag belongs to the pole it touches. A flag POINTS TO THE LEFT SIDE of its own pole if its cloth reaches out to the left of that pole's centre line, and POINTS TO THE RIGHT SIDE if its cloth reaches out to the right of it; each flag reaches to one side only. LEFT and RIGHT are the left and right of the page as you look at it, and each flag is judged against its own pole, not against the other pole or the middle of the page. The grey page frame, the grey corner ticks, the grey ground line and the grey clouds are decoration and carry no direction. Which side each flag reaches to is chosen separately from the flag colours, the pole heights, the pole positions, the size of each flag, how far each flag reaches, how far its tip droops and the clouds, so on some pages the two flags reach out to the same side and on other pages one reaches left while the other reaches right, and neither is a mistake. No image in this set is a borderline case: every flag reaches at least 40 pixels sideways from its own pole, so no flag hangs limp. Report the two flags in the picture in front of you, and do not answer from the usual assumption that one wind blows across a whole scene. Do the two flags reach out to the same side of their own poles, or to opposite sides? Answer exactly one of: same, opposite.
